title: Diamond Model
summary: The Diamond Model is an intrusion analysis framework that describes every malicious event as the interaction of four core features: an adversary, a capability, an infrastructure and a victim. The adversary is the actor or group directing activity. The capability is the tool, malware, exploit or credential the actor wields. The infrastructure is the physical or logical channel used to deliver the capability and control it, such as a domain, mail service, virtual private server or compromised host. The victim is the target, whether a person, organisation, account, asset or data set. Each event is drawn as a diamond with those four vertices. The value of the model lies in its edges and the pivots they permit: given any single known vertex, an analyst can reason about the others, and a confirmed link on one edge strengthens hypotheses along the rest. If two events share infrastructure and a capability but differ in victim, that suggests a broader campaign. If two share a victim and a capability but use different infrastructure, that suggests the actor is rotating channels defensively. The model also carries a socio-political meta-feature layer and, in the extended form, a technology meta-feature, acknowledging that adversary motivation and victim characteristics shape activity as much as tools do. Because the Diamond Model is event-centric, it complements rather than replaces kill-chain and ATT&CK views: it answers who did what to whom using what, while ATT&CK answers how. In practice, analysts use it to cluster events, generate collection requirements, prioritise intelligence gaps and document confidence. Its limits are equally important. The model is descriptive, so it imposes no analytic rigour by itself, and pivoting from infrastructure alone is prone to the same false attribution traps as any single-source inference.
objectives: You will be able to label the four Diamond Model vertices and the edges between them for a given intrusion report.
You will be able to pivot from a known infrastructure vertex to defensible hypotheses about capability and adversary.
You will be able to cluster multiple events into a campaign by comparing shared and divergent vertices.
You will be able to explain how the Diamond Model complements ATT&CK and kill-chain analysis instead of replacing them.
You will be able to identify intelligence gaps as missing vertices or unsupported edges and turn them into collection requirements.
You will be able to document an intrusion narrative that keeps observed events separate from inferential claims.
